questions.q: Per the finalization checklist, what should you do with any run you want to include in your final analysis?
options: Ensure it's recorded in the run log with complete metadata -- not cited 'from memory'
Only include runs that confirmed the original hypothesis
Re-run it one final time regardless of whether it's already complete
Remove it from the run log to simplify the report
questions.explain: The checklist explicitly requires every run going into the final analysis to be in the run log with complete metadata, not recalled from memory -- and explicitly warns against only including confirming runs.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend freezing and archiving a clearly labeled 'final' dataset, separate from the working directory?
options: Because quantum cloud providers require a separate archive by policy
Because working directories are automatically deleted after each session
To ensure certainty, during report writing, that you're checking numbers from the final decided-upon result rather than an earlier, superseded run
Because final datasets must be stored in a different programming language format
questions.explain: The lesson explains the concrete risk this avoids: accidentally re-deriving or double-checking a number against an earlier, superseded run instead of the final, intended result.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'experiment summary' document this lesson describes?
options: A public blog post announcing the capstone's results
The final report itself, submitted in place of Lesson 20's report
A legal disclaimer required before publishing any quantum result
A short working document extracting and organizing the key facts (hypothesis, runs, findings, uncertainties) to make writing the full report faster
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the experiment summary is not the final report -- it's a bridging document that makes Lesson 20 faster to write by pre-organizing the key facts.

questions.q: In the worked finalization, why were BOTH the original (confounded) and the retried (corrected) 5-qubit comparisons kept in the final dataset?
options: Because only confounded data is considered valid for publication
Because the discrepancy between them is itself part of the finding, demonstrating the confound was diagnosed and controlled for
Because keeping two datasets is required by every quantum cloud provider
Because the retried data was actually discarded, not kept
questions.explain: The worked example explains that retaining both results, with the discrepancy explained, is more informative than reporting only one -- consistent with Lesson 18's point about demonstrating real diagnostic work.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend writing down confound/limitation notes immediately at finalization time, rather than waiting until the full report is being written?
options: Because limitations sections are optional and can be skipped if not written immediately
The details are freshest and easiest to capture accurately right after finalizing, rather than being reconstructed from memory later under write-up pressure
Because confounds disappear from the data if not recorded within 24 hours
Because Lesson 20 does not actually require any limitations content
questions.explain: The lesson states this explicitly: capturing this language now is far easier than reconstructing it from memory during the report-writing phase, when time pressure is higher.
